[00:00:40] 3 Managing the psychological toll of working on existential risks [00:01:00] 4 Luisa and Spencer surveyed people working on existential risk [00:04:23] 5 How to sustain your motivation [00:11:13] 6 Why you shouldn’t read the news [00:23:54] 7 Why guilt isn’t an optimal source of motivation [00:36:28] 8 Breaking the boom-and-bust cycle of burnout [00:44:41] 9 Specialness and saviour complex [00:51:46] 10 If you’re certain we’re doomed, you’re overconfident [00:57:36] 11 We’re all (probably) going to die [01:03:50] 12 When loved ones think you’re weird [01:17:21] 13 How to balance impact and personal wellbeing [01:28:20] 14 What people report actually helps [01:53:49] 15 Spencer read 100 self-help books: here’s what works [01:59:40] Cold open [00:00:00] Spencer Greenberg: Often when people are doing things like constantly checking news that’s stressing them out, they’re engaging in kind of weird coping behaviours that actually don’t allow their brain to become more OK with the thing. Imagine you had a magic dial and you could control how much of different emotions you would feel. Take your fear: would you dial it down to zero? I think I’m prone to throwing more hours at things. That is not the best way to be more productive. It’s like thinking that the way that you win a race is by going at maximum speed at every single moment. No, that’s actually how you get injured or burn out. Failing to accept your limitations can actually be disastrous towards the goals that you care about. There’s actually a mathematical equation we came up with. It’s about how much value you produce, and it splits into three factors… Spencer is back — for a 5th time! [00:00:40] Luisa Rodriguez: Today I’m speaking with Spencer Greenberg . Spencer is the founder and CEO of clearerthinking.org and coauthor of the book The 12 Levers: The Complete Psychological Toolkit For Improving Your Life — which is actually being released today, so congratulations, Spencer. Thanks for coming on. Spencer Greenberg: Thanks so much for having me. Managing the psychological toll of working on existential risks [00:01:00] Luisa Rodriguez: So at 80,000 Hours, we ask people to think deeply about some genuinely very distressing things — pandemics, AI, human extinction, factory farming. But taking these issues seriously is very difficult for multiple reasons, including for me personally. They’re hard emotionally: we’re talking about suffering and death on an enormous scale. They’re also really hard to truly comprehend: I think the human brain struggles to actually fathom the things that we at 80K think might be true — everyone on Earth might die in the next decade or sooner, humans and other sentient beings might suffer extraordinarily at some point (or already). Even in the best case, the world might transform, maybe for the better, but beyond recognition in the span of a few years — which, despite that being a positive thing, I still find very scary. I think all of that makes thinking about these issues emotionally fraught and also epistemically fraught. And some of these issues are further exacerbated when you decide to spend your career trying to solve these problems. We have to grapple with the fact that we might be able to help, and every moment we spend playing board games or on vacation is time that we don’t spend trying to reduce existential risk or help animals that are suffering. There’s also just so much uncertainty about these risks, so we might kind of simultaneously believe our work has incredibly high stakes, but also maybe we’re wrong about the whole AI thing and we’re all wasting our careers. Some of us have to decide whether to have kids in the next few years, or delay or skip it entirely, because maybe the next few years could be the most important ones in our careers. And we have to grapple with the fact that we think AI, pandemics, factory farming, and other issues are massive world problems, when many of our friends and relatives don’t understand why we think that or don’t care enough to change their behaviour. And working on these problems can also be a source of incredible meaning, so there’s a big positive too, which we’ll talk about. But I think we want to give some airtime to the way that this is costly — both to kind of normalise some of these issues, to talk about some things that can help, and then also just to be like, “Thank you for working on these problems anyways. We see that you’re doing that, and it’s hard, and we would like to help how we can.” I guess to start, do any of these things resonate with you? Do you struggle with any of them personally? Spencer Greenberg: Yeah, they absolutely resonate with me. And I think we should acknowledge these are incredibly difficult topics to work on psychologically. You know, we have constantly changing things in the AI space. I can absolutely relate to the fear that this could go really badly on many different levels — from more benign harms to very severe harms, or even existential catastrophe. Topics like animal welfare, the amount of suffering involved is staggering, and even thinking about it can be really disturbing. So I absolutely relate to these things, and also say, yeah, these are challenging topics. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, nice. I’m glad that we’ll get to draw on both some of that life wisdom and then also a bunch of your learned expertise. Luisa and Spencer surveyed people working on existential risk [00:04:23] Luisa Rodriguez: You have a lot of expertise on self-improvement and trying to be a better, more flourishing person in general. But neither of us, I would say, are experts on the particular intersection of mental health and existential risk — though I think your book is super relevant, even though it’s not tailored to it. But to get a better sense of what issues come up for people working on x-risk, we did a bit of research ourselves: I spoke to a couple of therapists who mostly treat patients working on existential risks, and your team ran a survey for people working on very important but neglected global problems — so x-risks, factory farming, building the EA [effective altruism] community — and then we’ve got your book that also, again, is super relevant. To start, can you say a bit about the survey you ran ? Spencer Greenberg: Yeah. We surveyed people who work on these high-impact cause areas like existential risk and, as you mentioned, animal welfare and AI. We ended up getting about 60 to 110 respondents, depending on the question — because some were optional and some people dropped out during the survey. The basic questions we were asking about are: Do you experience psychological challenges in this work? How big are those challenges? What are the nature of those challenges? What kinds of things have you done that you think might be helpful to yourself, or that you think might help others? And yeah, I think we have a lot of really interesting results from that. Luisa Rodriguez: Can you say a bit about the headline results? Spencer Greenberg: Yeah. I’ll first note that these tended to be younger people that responded, typically aged about 25 to 45, and typically working for less than 10 years in the field. What we found is that very few people were suffering from what you might call a clinical disorder or generalised anxiety disorder or major depressive disorder, but the majority of people do seem to find this work psychologically challenging. So usually it doesn’t get to the point of full-blown depression or anxiety, but it doesn’t mean it’s easy. In fact, not only did most people say that they experience at least somewhat difficult psychological challenges around it, but many people have even considered leaving or reducing their work in it because of these challenges. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, that is kind of surprising, especially the last part: people have considered leaving their work but aren’t currently reporting depression and anxiety. Do you think there could be some other explanation, and people actually are experiencing some depression and anxiety? Or do you think maybe those two questionnaires aren’t really capturing what makes this so hard for people? Or it’s actually just not that hard, and people aren’t depressed or anxious as a result of these topics? Spencer Greenberg: Well, generalised anxiety disorder and major depressive disorder reflect certain patterns in the mind that can be really painful and difficult, but they don’t reflect all that can be really difficult psychologically. I think what we’re seeing here is that people are struggling psychologically; they’re just not getting to the point of having those particular disorders. When we ran the survey, we asked people which of a variety of different psychological challenges they face from a list. In fact, the median number selected was six different psychological challenges of doing this work. Forty-five percent said they at least considered cutting back or leaving, and also 52% said that it at least moderately hurts their effectiveness or productivity. So I think the answer is that people experience a lot of psychological challenges; they just usually aren’t these full-blown disorders. Luisa Rodriguez: Right. Were there any other findings that felt particularly surprising to you? Spencer Greenberg: One was that the most common challenges people said they faced — which are not necessarily the most severe, but it’s still interesting to look at — were difficulty switching off or having boundaries around work: 68% of people said they had trouble switching off after work. I think that actually really is an issue, because it elevates your stress level, makes it difficult to relax. I think that can actually, even if it doesn’t get to a full-blown disorder, have pretty negative consequences over the long run. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, yeah. What were the next couple of most common things? Spencer Greenberg: Imposter syndrome was really common, at 60%. For those of you that don’t know, that’s when you kind of secretly harbour the fear that you’re not good enough, or that you’re there by some kind of mistake and you know you shouldn’t really be there. And then we also have burnout: 59% said they had some experience with burnout, which can mean different things to different people. It can be a loss of motivation, it can just be feeling too stressed to function. So a wide range of things can contribute to burnout. Fifty-six percent said they experience guilt, and then 54% said they experience anxiety or worry around their work. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, OK. Those just feel like very high numbers to me. We’ll talk about most of those things, and a couple of others. Before we start getting into some of the concrete issues, can you say a bit more about the book? Kind of what it covers and your process for writing it? Spencer Greenberg: Yeah. So our new book — and we would really love for you to check it out if it sounds interesting — is called The 12 Levers: The Complete Psychological Toolkit For Improving Your Life . The idea behind it is that my coauthor, Jeremy Stevenson, and I studied over 100 of the most popular self-improvement books, and over 20 of the most used therapies — so cognitive behavioural therapy, but also many others. What we were looking for is them saying any kind of method or technique or telling you to do something to change your life, and we made a giant database of everything they said — which is almost 500 different techniques. And then our question was: what are all of the psychological strategies for improving your life? What’s the high-level meta pattern here? And I was worried we’d have 50 different high-level patterns, but actually, to my surprise, we were able to boil it down to just 12 high-level psychological strategies for improving your life. And that’s where the name of the book comes from, The 12 Levers . We also looked at the evidence for these different levers. And the goal of the book is to teach you about what each lever is, how you can use it effectively, and give you specific concrete steps to put it into action. Each lever has multiple techniques around it, sometimes there are even dozens, so we try to pick what we think are the most useful techniques around each lever. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, nice. Again, it’s helpful for all sorts of issues you might have, but I was kind of blown away when I was preparing for this interview. It’s just a very relevant toolkit for this subset of issues too. How to sustain your motivation [00:11:13] Luisa Rodriguez: Let’s talk about some of the specific issues that come up for people working on x-risks. Actually I kind of want to start with a slightly different point, which is that I actually had a high when I first started getting really bought into existential risks being real. I guess not just x-risks, but there being very pressing global problems that people weren’t tracking, and that plausibly could get a lot better. I think it felt like I learned something important and true about the world, and as a result I got to have this big opportunity to work on something high stakes that not many people were taking seriously. It felt exciting and it felt like an opportunity. And I think the ideas are also just intrinsically interesting, almost like a good sci-fi novel. So I think there’s something enjoyable about that, which I feel kind of strange and awkward about. But from the conversations I’ve had with therapists who work with people working on these issues, this is kind of a common experience. Did you have anything like this, or do you know people that did? Spencer Greenberg: I think it’s actually really common, because if you have new information that makes you feel like you have special knowledge that’s important to the fate of the world, that’s an incredibly attractive idea. And we can see that idea growing in popularity in many different domains, right? There’s nothing unique about these ideas in that way; people are drawn to special knowledge. In addition, it can really give meaning to life. Having the sense of, “There’s something important and meaningful for me to work on,” that can be really motivating. Furthermore, it can make you feel connected to a community if there’s other people involved; you can feel connected to that community through these shared ideas. So yeah, I think in a way it can be really appealing, while it could also be frightening if you kind of grapple with the gravity of it all. Luisa Rodriguez: According to some of the therapists I spoke to — and it seems like the survey backs this up — after learning about these ideas, starting to work on them, maybe some people have a bit of a high, but then people can start to experience a kind of chronic, low-grade emergency state. So kind of the threat system being perpetually on , because you’re regularly aware that humanity is under threat, or that factory farming is causing enormous unimaginable suffering right now, and we’re not really on track to solve these issues. I think this can come with kind of hypervigilance, and compulsive monitoring of news sites and X, and the sense that you can’t slow down or stop working — because things are on fire, and we don’t have that much time before things get catastrophically bad. Do you personally experience anything like this? Spencer Greenberg: I, for my whole life, have had the kind of mind that tends to look for things that could go wrong. So I’m a kind of worrier personality ; that’s always something that I’ve dealt with. And over the years I’ve improved tremendously on this, and it’s much less of a problem for me now than it was when I was younger. You know, like on the weekends I’d have trouble even relaxing or enjoying the weekend because I’d stress myself out with my thoughts. So I feel like I’ve found a number of tools that really help, but I do think that’s my fundamental disposition. Like I don’t ever expect to have a different brain that’s not a worrier brain, but I do expect to have tools that make it all kind of easier that I can continue to use. But I think, especially with topics like this — where they feel so big and important, where they feel like they’re changing, where people feel morally responsible to contribute — you’re going to find this at especially high rates, not just among people born with brains like me, but probably among a lot of other types of brains too. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah. Do you buy that this is a bad thing? I ask because there are plenty of things that I worry about in my day-to-day life that I give more worry than I think they deserve. But these problems are exceptionally big, and probably deserve more worry than we give them. If we were actually going to have worry that was proportionate to the size of the issue, how much anxiety is the right amount of anxiety? Spencer Greenberg: There’s a lot to unpack there. And if you go to cognitive behavioural therapy, let’s say for anxiety, an exercise sometimes that you’ll engage in is one where you consider the evidence. So they’ll be like, “You’re worried about this thing. You’re worried about how your friend didn’t text you back. What’s the underlying thought there?” Maybe the underlying thought is like, “Maybe my friend doesn’t like me anymore.” And then they’ll be like, “OK, why don’t you consider the evidence for and against?” You’ll consider the evidence for and against, and often people will feel better after that, and it will help them have more realistic thinking. And there’s a temptation, I think, if someone goes to a friend who doesn’t buy into these [existential risk] ideas, or even goes to a therapist who’s used to practicing that technique, where they’ll be like, “Consider the evidence.” And that’s actually really unhelpful in this situation, because chances are, if you’re listening to this podcast, you’ve already thought a lot about the evidence — and if someone’s like, “Consider the evidence for and against this problem that you think is a horrible problem being really bad,” you’re like, “Yeah, I’ve thought about the evidence, and I think it actually is really bad.” So that’s not the way to go in these kinds of situations, right? But I think it’s also important to ask the question, what is hypervigilance, and what’s the point of it? Effectively it’s a state that’s preparing you to take drastic action. Like there’s something dangerous that’s coming: you’ve got to go, you’ve got to act. Unfortunately, it’s really not a healthy state to be in all the time . It’s not good for your body, it’s not good for your mind. It can literally mess up things like digestion, because it actually affects your digestion when you’re in a hypervigilant state. You know, I like to think about professional athletes here. Do professional athletes want to be stressing their bodies all the time? If you’re training to be in the Olympics, and all you care about is the goal of winning the Olympics, are you just stressing your body to the absolute limit? The answer is absolutely no, because that is not the performance-optimising move. The performance-optimising move involves genuine rest; it involves variation of things. You’re not always working just on that one skill set. You’re going to have off days. You’re going to have days where you’re practicing other things or doing cross training or whatever — and that’s even if you just care about optimising for the goal. So I think we have to be realistic about like, what is this state, what is it doing for us? And what kind of beings are we realistically? Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, I think the “what kinds of beings are we realistically?” feels really important to me. Part of my brain thinks that I can just not be a human. I don’t know what gave me this idea. I think it is something about this community really valuing self-improvement and feeling like changing parts about yourself is kind of possible. I think some people think people can’t change, people can’t improve. Spending lots of time around the kinds of people who think they can make big improvements to the world, I think you also spend time around the kinds of people who think that they can better themselves — and that includes things like, “I can work harder; I can boost my productivity.” Spencer Greenberg: Well, I think there are a few issues going on here. One is that people can have a sense that the way they get social credit is by being the hardest worker or the one who’s doing the most good or whatever. If you’re in a community that values that, that can become a kind of optimisation metric — even to the point of it being unhealthy, and even past the point of it actually really being admired. It’s just sort of the sense that, “I’ll be admired more if I push this way.” And I think that can be an unhealthy dynamic of competing over who can grind themselves the hardest. I don’t think that is the way anyone would want the community to be. But sometimes, maybe people can perceive that, and that can have negative consequences. The other thing is that, even if your goal were just to get the maximum performance, you have to be realistic about what kind of body you have and what kind of mind you have — and grinding all the way is not actually the way to get maximum performance. It’s a naive version of trying to get maximum performance. It’s like thinking that the way that you win a race is by going at maximum speed at every single moment. No, that’s actually how you get injured or burn out, right? That’s not the way you win the race. Luisa Rodriguez: One thing that especially resonated with me was this idea that status is part of the motivation. I think I have this narrative that the reason I want to work harder is purely because of impact, but I think if I really reflect, you know, there is a part of me that wants people to think I work hard just because they’ll admire me more. And there’s a part of me that wants my manager to think I work hard because I want to be a good student. So why does this feel important? I think it feels important because when I try to interrogate why I find it so hard to rest, I think the main motivation is impact. But I think that the fact that actually these other motivations are in there feels important for me to notice — because really, deep down, it isn’t all about impact. Yeah, it feels like there’s something there. I don’t know. What do you think? Spencer Greenberg: Yeah. This goes back to the question of what kind of beings are we? I would argue that we’re beings with many different drives. And some of them are very low level — like generally people will avoid taking on extra effort unless they have some reason to. Literally they’ll walk in straight lines instead of curved lines, right? They’ll take the path of least resistance. Well, why is that? I think we have some drive to reduce energy expenditure. Of course, you can override it. You could have a goal that overrides it. But I think it’s worth noticing that that’s a drive. I actually think we have dozens of these drives. We have a drive to be accepted by our social community, probably because we would literally die if we weren’t 50,000 years ago. I think we have all these overlapping drives, and then we have this kind of reasoning, more rational part of our minds that’s coming up with principles to live by and ideas that we want to follow and things we believe in, et cetera — but that’s operating amidst all of these drives. It doesn’t override all these drives. And that actually can create a lot of internal conflict when the drives and that more rational part are not gelling that well. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, I want to come back to the internal conflict stuff. I think a lot of what we’re going to talk about today has to do with that. Before we do, I’m curious if there’s anything you found helpful in recognising and accepting that the type of person you are is a human with limitations. I just want to be the kind of being that can work as hard as my values make me feel like I should. Have you done anything, something like kind of dealing with the grief of it or something? Spencer Greenberg: Well, I mean, it is a very powerful idea, that we’re such limited beings, and that no matter how hard we work to be unlimited beings, we’re never going to get there. All of these things are just ideals that we strive for and we won’t come close. For example, I really care about trying to be rational, and I regularly see how far I am from that goal. And you could let that kind of undercut your motivation, being like, “Oh man, I’m so far from that,” or you can turn that around and you can say, “Hey, I can keep becoming a better version of myself and move incrementally towards this more ideal form.” And that can be exciting. I don’t think it has to be demotivating. It can be motivating, actually: being limited, but seeing how you can progress and improve. But I would also say that failing to accept your limitations can actually be disastrous towards the goals that you care about. So the more accurately you can see yourself — what you are, what your limitations are — the better you can be at all the things that you care about. Denying them is actually a strategy that’s going to undercut you. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, totally. Why you shouldn’t read the news [00:23:54] Luisa Rodriguez: I guess there are a couple of threads there, and I want to put pins in a few of them and stay on this idea of the threat system always being on, and that being a thing that can feel maybe truth tracking and important — because in some ways it feels like the world is genuinely on fire — but also not good for you as a human being. Not good for your work, if you assume something like… Actually, not just assume: I believe that it is probably just bad for your work if your threat system is always on and you are constantly feeling chronically on fire. One common way that people end up entering this threat system and staying in it is tracking world events. So maybe there’s the release of a new model that seems super impressive, or a blog post or an interview with someone talking about how AI timelines are even shorter than they thought, or bad news about policy, AI regulation stuff. What approach seems most helpful to you in handling these kinds of triggers? Spencer Greenberg: I’ll use a parallel because I think it’s helpful: news consumption broadly. Many people find news of the world stressful because the news tends to focus on bad things, and also there’s bad things happening in the world. So they read an article on X and they’re like, “Ahhh, things are falling apart!” And then a friend posts on Facebook and they’re like, “Ahh!” So my strategy for helping deal with this challenge is I subscribe to a service that just gives one news story a day, and that is my news. Basically the idea is: if it’s not important enough to be the top news story of the day, it’s probably not important enough to care about. And in fact, funnily enough, many days that’s not even important enough for me to want to read it, and you know, they’re picking one news story a day. It’s kind of crazy to think about, but so much of this is noise, right? And I find that helpful for me: staying on top of the important things happening in the world, but not getting sucked into it and not wasting time, and you’re not getting stressed out about things needlessly, but still knowing kind of what’s happening. Now, let’s say you’re in the field of AI, and things are moving so fast. It may be even more difficult to deal with, just because there is information you really want to stay on top of and it is changing a lot. And there, I would say the same kind of strategy can be useful: being really aware of where am I getting my news, what are the good news sources, what’s the stuff that’s going to keep me up to date? And then trying to block out all the noise, right? You don’t need to constantly scroll down and get every single new post on X about AI, a bunch of which are probably complete exaggerations anyway or bad takes. You know, figure out your trusted news sources and that’s where you’re going to get your information. That’s how you can stay on top of things, and then you don’t need to just constantly passively consume all this other information. Luisa Rodriguez: Why do you think people are so inclined to doomscroll? Spencer Greenberg: Well, it’s a bit of an irony, because often people go to social media as a form of avoidance or as a form of attempting to unwind, right? So they’re like, “I don’t want to think about this thing. I’m stuck on this thing. Let me open up social media.” Or like, “I’ve just been working hard, let me unwind.” And the irony is that they end up often in this sort of hypervigilant state when they’re on social media, where it’s like not even necessarily doing a good job of getting them to relax, or maybe they’ve avoided this one thing and now they’re stressed out about this other thing they’re looking at. So it often doesn’t serve the purpose that it’s intended to. This actually connects to an idea from our book, The 12 Levers . In our beta testing, we were having people read the book. This idea is one of these ideas that our beta testers just kept bringing up, like this was an unlock for them. It’s this idea that we call “glad you did it” activities. The idea is that often we do things that are serving some need, or that we believe are serving some need — like rest, relaxation, et cetera — but when we actually really get down to it, we could swap them with a different activity that serves the same need, but afterwards you’re like, “I’m glad I did that.” You’re not like, “That was a giant waste of time.” I think a mistake people often make is that they try to swap out those activities with things that don’t serve that need. So you as a human have a need to rest, but what you might be doing to rest is going and scrolling social media — which, you know, maybe it is a little bit restful, but maybe it doesn’t even serve that person very well, and then afterwards you’re probably like, “Why did I do that? That was not a good use of time.” Well, what else is restful? What else shares that same need? Maybe walking your dog or going for a walk in nature or having a call with a friend or whatever it is. And maybe it takes a little bit more planning to make that happen; it’s not quite as mindless — but if you could swap it out with something that serves the same need at least as well, hopefully better, but where afterwards you’re like, “I’m glad I did that; that was a good use of time,” it can not only serve our needs better, but actually make life more meaningful and fulfilling, and I think be more restorative so you are more ready when now you have to go take action in the future. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, nice. I can imagine that’s in contrast to what maybe I’d be tempted to do if I had this problem of doomscrolling. I’m actually not a doomscroller. I am a scroller, but I’m not a doomscroller. I think I’d be tempted to be like, “A virtuous thing would be to work” or do something that’s a good use of time according to unrealistic values. It feels like a really key thing about this is it’s meeting the rest need; it’s not meeting the goal of “be a more productive person all the time.” Spencer Greenberg: Exactly, exactly. And that’s a mistake people constantly make. They’re trying to swap one need for another, which often doesn’t work. You need to do meaningful work, that’s great, but you’re trying to replace your need to rest, and it doesn’t satisfy your need to rest. It’s a different thing. And actually, you can kind of grind yourself to a pulp and make it hard for you to function if you’re never letting yourself actually satisfy that rest need. Or if your “rest” is not actually restful, like you’re actually stressed out doing your rest because you’re scrolling stressful AI news or whatever it is. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, that makes tonnes of sense. One need that people are trying to get met is rest. It feels like for some people there probably is another. I’m kind of just guessing, because this isn’t a problem I relate to as much, but I wonder if there’s something like, “This is a true thing about the world. It’s scary. I need to look at it. I need to know the true thing so that I can be able to track it, and not be snuck up on or something.” It’s like wanting to watch a danger approach because it feels safer, even though that’s triggering the threat system. Does that sound plausible? Spencer Greenberg: Absolutely. When people feel like there’s a frightening thing in the world, they’ll often track it. You look at early days of the COVID pandemic, people were absolutely glued to any source of information, couldn’t talk about anything else. And I think it is that vigilant system of like, “This really scary thing is there. We’ve all got to monitor it really closely.” And that goes back to some of what we were talking about before: you need a system for monitoring it. That is important if that’s your field, if that’s what you’re focused on. But once you have that in place, it actually can give you permission to not monitor other times, right? But if you don’t have a good system in place, then you might always feel like “I might miss something critical” or “I might need to monitor” because you don’t trust that it will be monitored. It actually reminds me of this idea of the Getting Things Done productivity system, where oftentimes when people have never done complex work before, they have very ad hoc systems for keeping track of things, so they never really are sure that they’re on top of what needs to be on top of, or that all their to-dos are there. And one of the insights of Getting Things Done is: have a single trusted system. Anytime you have something to do, it goes in the trusted system, so you know you will never miss it. And that just removes the need for this vigilance of like, “But what if I missed this thing?” blah, blah. You’re like, “No, I just have this one system, and it will always tell me what I need to do.” Luisa Rodriguez: Cool. And so the version of that that kind of applies to these kinds of risks is: in your case, figure out what news you want to receive, and know that you’ll know about the worst thing that’s happening in the world. So at least I would consider whether you’re sort of accidentally pretending that you believe in objective moral truth because you don’t know what else to do, and I’d say that there is something to ground that in. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, I think you’re probably actually describing me, so I’m really tempted to dig into it more, but we just don’t have time. Let’s say that lots of people listening do either think it is objectively true that we should value other people’s wellbeing, other beings’ wellbeing; or that it isn’t objectively true, but that we value it, as individuals with values for complicated psychological reasons. My impression is that you think valuism is kind of good either way. It leads to good outcomes. It leads to you being a pretty flourishing person that can also do really good work to help others, help solve global problems. Can you make that case? Spencer Greenberg: Absolutely. First of all, things like existential risk are incredibly bad according to almost everyone’s values. So even if everyone were valuists, in the hypothetical thought experiment, I think they would be taken incredibly seriously, far more seriously than society takes them today, and there’d be a significant amount of effort to reduce existential risk. And I think many if not all of the effective altruism cause areas would also be extremely high priority to people with a valuist philosophy. Not everyone, because people’s values differ, but almost everyone has values around reducing suffering. They don’t want even strangers, people they’ve never met, to suffer. They don’t want animals to suffer. It’s not the biggest value for most people, but it’s a significant value for almost everyone. So I do think valuism kind of gets you to similar places as effective altruist thinking. However, I also think that it is less likely to grind you to a pulp than philosophies like utilitarianism. And this is not a claim about being true or not, I’m just talking about the psychological effects of it. If you really deeply buy into it, I think it can have very strongly negative psychological effects, and it can be very prone to causing you to burn out — which is kind of ironic, because if it were the true theory, it would suck if believing the true theory causes you to not be good at acting on the true theory because you burn out. But that might actually be the case. Luisa Rodriguez: Right. Can we talk through an example that illustrates how one might make decisions when values conflict? Spencer Greenberg: Yes. I think it’s good to focus on a simple example to illustrate the principles. Imagine that your friend writes a play and invites you to see it. And afterwards, they come up to you and say, “What did you think?” And you can tell they just want you to say nice things about it, they want you to say that you really loved it. But the fact is you absolutely hate it. You can’t even think of a single good thing to say about it. It’s so bad from your perspective. What do you do? I think most people are going to feel conflicted in this situation. On the one hand, they want to be truthful. Most people have a value of being truthful, not spreading lies. And let’s assume that it’s not better for your friend to hear their play sucked. Let’s assume that they’re just going to feel bad. There’s no benefit that’s going to accrue. But on the other side of the ledger, you don’t want to cause your friend emotional pain. That sucks. Almost everyone has the value of not causing people emotional pain as well, right? So what do you do? The answer will differ for different people, depending on the relative strengths of those two values. So there’s not going to be a single answer to this question. So how do you even think about this? How do you kind of get traction on this? What I like to do is little mini thought experiments here. You could be like, suppose you knew your friend was going to be so depressed by what you said that they were going to go into a tailspin and not be able to function for a month. To me, then it’s an easy choice. Yes, I really care about truth, but that’s just not worth it. That’s too much emotional suffering to cause that to preserve the truth. Well, what if you had to give like a five-minute lie where you’re just going to make up all kinds of details that are not true about your thought process, blah, blah? Well, that would just be beyond the pale on a truth level, right? So you can begin, through these thought experiments, to kind of converge to where you sit. Because some of these will be obvious which one wins here, and then as you get closer and closer to the real situation, you’re going to be like, “OK, yeah, I think on this one I’m leaning here.” That’s the best way I know of in these practical situations to try to get to it: you start tweaking the parameters to see how your values react to that. We’re constantly facing values tradeoffs, because even at the very basic level, spending time on one thing to get one value means we spend less time on other values. When we really neglect values that are extremely important to us, I think that they start to pull harder, and we start paying a higher and higher psychological price to not having them met. And I think this is what happens when someone is all-in on the mission, and only thinks about the mission and doesn’t take into account their other values: they start to pull harder on them psychologically, and I think that leads to things like burnout. I think one of the causes of burnout is neglecting your other important values. One thing I think is really interesting about the effective altruism community — and this is how I frame it as a valuist, which is different than how other people frame it — is I think it’s a community more than anything that’s bonded together by having really strong values around reducing suffering and increasing happiness broadly for all conscious beings, and really strong values around truth. So it’s kind of fascinating to me how often effective altruists think in utilitarian terms. Utilitarianism doesn’t care about truth. You know, in theory someone could be like, “I’m going to lie for utilitarian ends.” But actually, this is a community that cares deeply about the truth also. And I think that’s not at all captured in sort of the utilitarian ethos, but it is captured in almost everything the effective altruism community does. It’s very truth oriented. So I would say it’s a community with these two really strong values, and that’s kind of what unites it. Luisa Rodriguez: It feels like part of what happens for people who end up really struggling with not meeting, not putting some weight on these alternative values, alternative to making the world better for others, is something like not a commitment to being honest with themselves about what’s going to happen if they don’t put some weight on those other values. It feels like it’s kind of a failing to be realistic about the fact that we in fact are humans. And whether it’s the ideal thing philosophically, whether it’s ideal for the world or not, clearly, descriptively, we value things — we value our loved ones, we value spending time with others, we value leisure. It feels like a way in for me on this has been that I just was trying way too hard to reject reality and reject my own humanity. I was like, “No, I can just sacrifice all of my other values for this one particular value of making the world better.” And maybe that’ll land for some other people, because we are so interested in truth. The reality is that we have things that pull us, and that really start messing with our wellbeing when we ignore them. And just from a truth-tracking perspective, we should be honest about what those are, and be willing to incorporate that into our worldview and how we act. Spencer Greenberg: Right. To reinforce what you said, even if you think there’s an objective moral truth, and you think you know what it is and you plan to pursue that, there’s still psychological facts about who you are as a being. And if you think that your actual value system places equal value on the suffering of a mouse as it does the suffering of your mother, then unless you have a really bad relationship with your mother, then you’re very likely deluding yourself. So it’s important to understand what kind of being you are, what you actually value. Even if you don’t fundamentally care about those values, I think you’ll pay a very significant price to not understand your values. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah. So the thing that’s been really helpful for me is Internal Family Systems , which I think some people call “parts work.” You’re kind of introspecting to figure out what different parts of you want, which feels really symmetric with the thing that you’re describing: you’ve got different values, and you’re trying to figure out how to weight them. Like if you picture a boardroom or a group of children who all have different singular personalities — one might be ambitious, one might be very fearful — and these different parts can kind of represent a value that you have. I’m curious if you’ve used anything like parts work to try to make life decisions where values are in tension? Spencer Greenberg: Yeah. In our book, The 12 Levers , we have a whole section on this. I will just say that “parts work” is kind of a broader umbrella term; there are actually multiple different therapies that use this concept, including schema therapy , self-compassion-focused therapy, and then also Internal Family Systems, which you mentioned. So I just want to be clear that it’s kind of a broader concept. The way I like to think about it is that we have these kind of bundles of wants, thoughts, values, urges, et cetera that come together. When you have that, you could start kind of dialoguing with that part of you. You can think of that as a part of you. I would not take this literally, and I think sometimes people do take this too literally. It’s not like you literally have these different parts, but I think it can be a useful way to explore yourself. And different versions of parts work do it differently, but the classic general technique is you want to notice that there’s some part of you that wants something or has urges or needs not met. You can give it a name. It can be helpful to give it a name, because then you can talk about it or refer to it later. So maybe you’ll say, like, “I’m going to call it the Critic. It’s the part of me that tells me I’m never doing enough, I’m never good enough.” And then you want to put yourself into a state where you can talk to it very compassionately, without being reactive. And they give different names to this, like the Self or the Compassionate Self or the Adult or whatever it is. But you’re kind of going to be dialoguing with this part from a very compassionate, healthy state, and you’re going to try to just explore what that part needs and wants and cares about, and try to help it have its needs met. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah. The way that I found it useful that’s relevant is, using your play example, I might have two parts: one part that really values honesty and one part that really values not hurting people’s feelings. And probably the honesty part would be like, “Ugh, I really don’t want to say something untrue. I feel really strongly that we don’t say untrue things.” And the part that values not hurting people’s feelings is like, “But it’s going to hurt them so much if I say that I thought the play was trash!” And by putting them directly in dialogue, often what happens is I end up being like, to that part of me that values honesty, “I appreciate you. I’m glad that you are here asking me to be an honest person. I agree that’s really important. But do you understand? Can you get on board with doing this thing that in this case we think is more important, which is not hurting people’s feelings? It just seems like in this case that’s the win.” And that part is like, “Oh fine, like I appreciate you hearing me out, but yes, we can do that.” It feels like there’s something like that part needed to be heard, otherwise it’s going to keep screaming at me, like, “But you weren’t honest! But you weren’t honest!” And I feel like this gives it space to, one, say its piece so that it doesn’t keep screaming at me, and two, for me to grieve that I didn’t give that part what it wanted. And it feels like this ends up being a useful tool for me. You know, I think I had to kind of grieve the part of me that wanted to work 80-hour weeks because it thought that was the most morally good thing to do in order to fulfil the wishes of the part of me that really wanted to be a mom. And I think that part of me that wanted to work harder would have just kept being like, “You’re a bad person! You’re a bad person!” unless I’d really heard it out and been like, “I hear you. Thank you. You want me to be a good person, I appreciate that. But I’ve decided, full-eyed looking honestly at things, that I want to be a mom anyways.” Does that make sense? Spencer Greenberg: Absolutely. And I think when we have something tugging at us, whether it’s an unmet value or an emotion that we’re kind of ignoring and suppressing, I think it can keep pulling harder and harder. And sort of staring at it face-on, and really accepting that this is something that matters or this is an emotion that you’re feeling, may actually help reduce the pull of it once it’s really acknowledged. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah. What people report actually helps [01:53:49] Luisa Rodriguez: OK, let’s talk about some things from the survey that people said helped. I think you asked a couple different questions that hit on this. One was just what helped the most. Another question was, “Imagine someone similar to you is about to start working in the same cause area as you. Knowing what you know now, if they wanted your advice related to psychological and mental health aspects of this kind of work, what would you tell them?” What were some of the things that came up that you think might be most helpful to people listening? Spencer Greenberg: First, there were a lot of the usual suspects of what people said helped. If we look at people who said they tried a thing, and then what percentage of those wrote about it when we asked what was the most helpful, we find that at the top of the list are: therapy, medication, talking to friends and family about the issues. Those really stood out: among those that tried them, they were more likely to say that they were really helpful. But I actually think a lot of the most instructive stuff was around when we asked the question, “What would you advise someone who’s very similar to you who’s getting into this field, in terms of dealing with these psychological challenges?” And there I think it surfaced some interesting recommendations. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, I’d love to talk through those. What’s one of them? Spencer Greenberg: Many people talked about sustainability, and how focusing on sustainability is really important. Even if you don’t think it matters for its own sake, it’s really important just to be effective. And people that are very focused on sacrifice rather than sustainability often aren’t even able to achieve the thing they want. In other words, sacrifice doesn’t work over the long term, leads to boom-and-bust cycles, or they burn out and they end up having to leave or change their work. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, this one’s interesting, because I think some people in the community kind of react suspiciously to sustainability as a concept — I think because maybe they worry people are using motivated reasoning to convince themselves they can have things that are kind of self-indulgent. And I feel like there’s a concept we’ve talked about in another episode that’s useful, which is that sometimes there are multiple reasons for doing something, and meeting certain values that seem kind of selfish might be selfishly good and it also might be instrumentally good. And the fact that it is selfishly good doesn’t mean that it is incorrect that it is instrumentally good for achieving goals like helping others thrive. And I feel like the sustainability thing just seems really empirically true for a lot of people, and even though it also is nice because it means you get to prioritise your wellbeing more, I think too many people make that a reason that probably we should be suspicious of people saying that sustainability is important. Spencer Greenberg: In my experience, being totally adherent to a philosophy can actually increase people’s self-deception around this. If you think that everything has to be justified in terms of maximising utility, then now, given your nature as a human being, you have tremendous psychological pressure to justify everything that is for something else you care about in terms of maximising utility. And I think that’s actually a very unhealthy and self-deluded state to be in. But if you accept, “Wait, I’m a human. I have multiple values, and here’s what I actually value,” then you can talk about, like, “Actually, the reason I have my friends is because I value human connection, it’s really important to me, and they bring me joy, not because it makes me more effective.” Just being more both understanding yourself psychologically better empirically and being more honest with yourself. Luisa Rodriguez: Nice. Yeah, I think that’s really insightful. What was another thing people said? Spencer Greenberg: People really encourage others to have life outside of the work. In other words, to build relationships that are not just all people in the community. You know, I live in New York where people talk about AI a lot less. But when I’ve visited the Bay Area, there have been times I’ve been shocked about how you can’t have a single conversation not about AI, even at social events. I’m like, do people ever talk about other things? That can feel oppressive, like you just need a break right from that. So yeah, I do think that this is wise: maintaining relationships outside of people in the community, that can give you a break, that can give you like a playful experience that’s not just about work. Because maybe when you’re socialising with people who also prioritise these topics, there’s a natural tendency for them to come up all the time, even when you’re supposed to be doing restful things. Luisa Rodriguez: Nice. Yeah. Were there others that seemed good? Spencer Greenberg: Another really key one that I think is really insightful that people pointed to is: don’t wait until things have fallen apart. Be preventative about taking care of yourself. Notice the earliest signs of pre-burnout. Don’t wait until it’s burnout. Like, “I’m noticing I have a bit less motivation here. I’m noticing that I’m waking up stressed every day, or I’m having trouble sleeping.” And then take preventative action — whether that’s seeing a therapist, seeing a coach, just doing self-improvement techniques to try to improve that situation — and not saying, “Well, I can live with this bad sleep, I can live with this feeling of stress all the time, I can live with this lower motivation.” Maybe, but is it going to get worse, and how long can you actually live with it? And also, you don’t necessarily have to live with it. You can have a more pleasant lifestyle. You don’t have to necessarily suffer so much, and you still might be able to be equally or more effective. Luisa Rodriguez: Nice. Yeah, I think those are really good. Spencer read 100 self-help books: here’s what works [01:59:40] Luisa Rodriguez: OK, let’s talk a bit about your book. A bunch of the tools we’ve been talking about here, maybe all of them really, are touched on in your book, The 12 Levers . Very high level, what motivated you to write it? Spencer Greenberg: So throughout my life I’ve found a lot of value in specific self-improvement methods that have really been transformative for me. At the same time, I’ve read so much self-improvement where I felt like I just didn’t really get much out of that — like it didn’t really have any useful techniques, or it could be that it sort of repeats other things. So the space felt like a bit of a mess. Like, I know there’s really valuable stuff there, but it’s sort of hard to find it. And my coauthor, Jeremy Stevenson — who’s a clinical psychologist, he treats patients, and he also has a PhD in psychology — had really similar experiences, where he’d found some stuff transformative, but it’s hard to find the good stuff. So we both had this desire of like, “What is all the good stuff?” So we decided to join forces on this quest to find all the good stuff that we can, package it, try to understand what’s there, try to synthesise it, try to get the meta patterns out of it, and also look at the evidence. So we actually reviewed the evidence on each lever, and we have a sort of appendix at the back of the book that talks about the evidence for each lever. What I think I like best about the book is that I think every one of the 12 levers can be really useful, so it’s kind of a toolkit that you can come back to in different life situations and say, “Right now in life, I think I really need Lever 5.” And you can go read that and get really concrete instructions of ways to apply that. But another time in life you might need Lever 11 or Lever 2. So it’s trying to give you these tools that you can come back to again and again for many different things. That’s why, even though this is not a book about dealing with psychological challenges of high-impact work, I think it’s relevant — because I think it’s relevant to all psychological challenges. That is kind of the point of the book. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah. Nice. Is there a lever that you’ve personally found most useful in your life? Spencer Greenberg: Yeah. For me, we have a lever we call “approach the monster,” which is about the natural human tendency to run away from negative emotions, especially fear. The nature of fear is that we want to avoid it. If you think about it, that’s sort of how it operates. You know, you see a lion at the watering hole, and you don’t go back to the watering hole for a while, because you’re afraid of it. That’s a protective measure. But for many people, this process goes a bit haywire, and they start avoiding things due to negative emotions or anxiety or fear, and that actually causes all kinds of negative consequences in their life. And for me, that was huge, because I grew up with a lot of social anxiety — to the point where if I had to go start a conversation with a stranger at, let’s say, a party, I would feel like my heart was going to explode. It would be pounding so hard in my chest that I could barely function. And then when I would host events, because I enjoyed hosting events, I would get so nervous that I’d be stressed out the entire day beforehand, not able to enjoy the day before the event. Then when I was in my early 20s, I was like, “I’ve got to do something about this. I can make this better.” And I went to a therapist and he taught me about exposure therapy, which is a really effective method. He would give me these funny homework assignments like, “OK, this weekend you’re going to go to a bar and you’re going to strike up a conversation with five strangers, alone.” And I found this just so frightening, but we started small with the idea that I’m just going to go up and ask them the time. Like, I could do that, right? It was still scary to me, but it felt bearable. If I had to go in and just immediately start a conversation, maybe that would be too much, but it started easy. And then it would build up. It would be like, “What drink are you drinking? That looks good.” You know, it could build up to there, which is a little more stressful for me. Then eventually it culminated in really wacky exercises where I would go up to men I didn’t know and say, “Hey, would you mind giving me a hug?” And my brain predicted that I was going to get punched in the face, that they were going to get really angry at me. And the funny thing is, nobody had a bad reaction. Now, I’m not recommending you do this. Maybe in your area they would have a bad reaction. But in New York at the time, nobody had a bad reaction. I just thought that was so funny, because the difference between what my brain predicted and what happened was so huge. Luisa Rodriguez: Right. Yeah. Nice. A thing that you said, that feels like I’ve had to learn and relearn it, is: exposure therapy seems incredibly helpful, but I always make the mistake of not starting small enough, and then I almost learn the wrong lesson. I’m like, “Oh, the thing was as scary as I thought.” But I think it’s kind of surprising how small you have to start. Especially the scarier the thing, I think the more true that is. Proper exposure therapy I think really requires you to do a thing that is not going to crush you. And I think lots of people try to just be like, “OK, I’m just going to expose myself to the hard thing that I’m afraid of,” instead of like, “What is a small version that’s going to feel tolerable?” Spencer Greenberg: Yeah, intriguingly, there’s the two opposite ends of the spectrum. There’s gradual exposure, which is where you build up — which is what I would recommend for almost everyone — and then there’s flooding, where you start at the other end: you just do the most intense, difficult thing. And interestingly enough, flooding — where you do the most intense, difficult thing — actually can work, and it might even work faster. But here the challenge is that a lot of people do things during flooding that’s kind of screwing up the lesson and make it not work. So that’s why I don’t recommend it. First of all, a lot of people aren’t willing to do it because it’s so frightening. But it’s prone to people doing things during it that cause the wrong learning. For example, freaking out and running away, which could reinforce the fear, or engaging in massive coping mechanisms during it. So that’s why it’s usually not recommended. Luisa Rodriguez: Right. Because then you only learn that the thing is OK because you did the weird coping thing that you actually don’t want to do every time. Spencer Greenberg: Exactly. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, makes sense. Is there a lever that you’ve seen be most transformative for other people? Or is it hard to kind of narrow down to one? Spencer Greenberg: It’s so specific to what someone’s dealing with. But if I had to point people to one… Let’s say you have a problem in life. You’re struggling with it, you haven’t been able to solve it. The lever that I would point many people to in that case is the first lever, which is about unravelling the deeper hidden causes of an issue. It’s just really fascinating how often we understand the problems in our life at a fairly surface level of causality. Where we think, “My problem is that I get in fights with my spouse. That’s my problem.” And then you’re like, “OK, why do you get in fights with your spouse?” “Well, we’ll get in fights because they want X and I want Y.” “But a lot of other spouses have that situation where one of them wants one thing, one of them wants the other, and they don’t fight about it. So why are you fighting?” And there’s these deeper and deeper levels of causation. And we give a number of different techniques in that lever of how exactly do you get to the causality? But as you get deeper and deeper into causality, it often really helps you be much more effective at solving the problems of your life, and it’s very easy to notice that you’re not at the deepest level of causality. Luisa Rodriguez: Right. So for the husband and wife, it’s something like, actually they’re seeing these disagreements in some way that feels very hurtful or personal attack-y or something. And as you keep going deeper, you realise it’s not quite about the disagreement, it’s about feeling attacked? Is that…? Spencer Greenberg: Yeah. Oftentimes interpersonal disagreements like that that are recurring are not about the thing that they seem to be about. There’s a deeper thing that they’re about, like maybe it’s, “I just don’t feel like you really love me. I just am unconvinced that you love me or something like that.” You might be fighting about the dishes, but it’s really… And then it’s like, “Well, maybe I need to show my love for you in more ways that help it sink in more. What would do that for you?” You know what I mean? I like to think about, imagine your car won’t start, right? And you just start trying things at random. You’re like “Maybe if I refill the gas. Oh, that didn’t work. Maybe if I fix the battery. That didn’t work.” It’s like you have to understand what’s wrong with the car to fix it effectively. Picking things at random is usually not very effective. A mechanic is going to diagnose it. It’s like that, but for the problems in your own life. Luisa Rodriguez: Nice. OK, last question: which lever do you find that you’ve had to kind of keep relearning? So you find it really helpful, but it’s just really hard to make it stick, maybe because the kinds of problems it helps with are the kinds that you struggle with most. Spencer Greenberg: Lever 8 is about how to be more productive. And we call that “tuning the productivity equation.” There’s actually a mathematical equation we came up with; it’s actually literal. It’s about how much value you produce, and it splits into three factors: The time you put in: the more time you put into something, all else equal, you’re going to produce more of what you value The efficiency: how much [output] do you produce per hour The importance of the thing you’re working on: if it’s not important to you at all, according to what you value, you get no output in terms of what you value. And I think that very often people who want to be productive throw hours at the problems — because in a way, it’s the simplest and most obvious. And it does improve your productivity, as long as you can keep the other things equal. But in many cases — unless you’re underworking, that’s one thing — but for many productive people, it’s actually the worst way to get more productivity. And I think I’m prone to throwing more hours at things, so that’s one that I have to keep coming back to and be like, that is not the best way to be more productive, and remind myself of it. So it’s an ongoing piece of work for me. Luisa Rodriguez: Yeah, I feel like we could have spent a bunch of time talking about that one, and it’ll be interesting to a lot of people listening. So yeah, I encourage people to pick up the book . It is available today. My guest today has been Spencer Greenberg. Thank you so much for coming on, Spencer. Spencer Greenberg: Thanks so much for having me. Really fun conversation.

title: VF Corporation Delivered First Quarter Fiscal 2027 Ahead of Guidance
summary: July 29, 2026 6:00am EDT - Raises full year revenue outlook to +2% or better C$ vs. LY Appoints Abhishek Dalmia as Chief Financial Officer and Chief Operating…
body_text: VF Corporation Delivered First Quarter Fiscal 2027 Ahead of Guidance Download as PDF July 29, 2026 6:00am EDT Related Documents Audio Earnings Webcast Earnings Presentation PDF Raises full year revenue outlook to +2% or better C$ vs. LY Appoints Abhishek Dalmia as Chief Financial Officer and Chief Operating Officer DENVER--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- VF Corporation (NYSE: VFC) today reported financial results for its first quarter (Q1'27) ended June 27, 2026 ahead of guidance and raises full year revenue outlook. The Company's Board of Directors authorized a quarterly per share dividend of $0.09. These financial results are also reflected in a presentation available on the Investor Relations website at ir.vfc.com. Bracken Darrell, President and CEO, said: "We had a solid start to the year, beating our revenue and operating income guidance. The North Face® , Timberland® and Altra® delivered another quarter of growth; and Vans® Americas DTC continued to grow but was more than offset by declines in global Wholesale. We expect Vans® Wholesale to improve significantly in the second half of the year. Given our overall Q1 performance and better visibility into the balance of the year, we are raising our FY'27 revenue guidance." Darrell continued, “Regarding our CFO transition announced today, I would like to thank Paul for his partnership, leadership and contributions to VF. Looking ahead, I’m excited for Abhishek to step into his newly expanded role of Chief Financial Officer and Chief Operating Officer. body_text: Vestis Announces Date for Fiscal Third Quarter 2026 Results Conference Call and Webcast July 28, 2026 7:00 AM EDT Download as PDF ATLANTA--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Vestis (NYSE: VSTS), a leading provider of uniforms and workplace supplies, today announced that it will issue its fiscal third quarter 2026 results before the market opens on Tuesday, August 11, 2026. A conference call will be held that same morning at 8:30 a.m. ET to review the Company’s financial results and conduct a question-and-answer session. A webcast of the conference call and accompanying presentation materials will be available in the Investor Relations section of the Company’s website at https://ir.vestis.com . To listen to a live broadcast, go to the site at least 15 minutes prior to the scheduled start time in order to register, download, and install any necessary audio software. To participate in the live teleconference: United States Live : 800-267-6316 International Live : 203-518-9783 Access Code: VSTSQ326 A replay of the live event will also be available on the Company’s website shortly after the conclusion of the call. About VESTIS™ Vestis is a leader in the B2B uniform and workplace supplies category. Vestis provides uniform services and workplace supplies to a broad range of North American customers from Fortune 500 companies to locally owned small businesses across a broad set of end sectors. The Company’s comprehensive service offering primarily includes a full-service uniform rental program, floor mats, towels, linens, managed restroom services, first aid supplies, and cleanroom and other specialty garment processing. title: Cómo cobrar de Deel (2026). Guía sobre métodos de retiro, comisiones y plazos
summary: Cómo cobrar de Deel y recibir tus ingresos de la mejor manera. Métodos, comisiones y plazos de cobro.
body_text: Conclusiones clave Elegir bien tu método de retiro evita perder dinero en Deel. Deel opera en más de 150 países y ofrece 15 formas de cobro. La Deel Card cobra 0,75 % (máximo 25 $) para Estados Unidos y 2 % (máximo 15 $) para los demás países. Wallbit te ofrece una cuenta global para cobrar tus pagos de Deel sin comisiones. Si trabajas para el exterior, es probable que conozcas la plataforma de pago de nómina Deel , una de las más usadas por empresas de todo el mundo para pagar a trabajadores remotos que exportan servicios. Hasta hace dos años, la empresa tenía un valor aproximado que superaba los 12.000 millones de dólares . Si te pagan a través de esta plataforma, la forma en que configures tu retiro define cómo llega el dinero a tu cuenta y cuánto te va a costar . Por eso, en esta guía veremos cómo funciona Deel, qué métodos de retiro existen, cuánto cobra cada uno, y cómo recibir tu dinero en Wallbit sin perder dinero en comisiones. ¿Qué es Deel? Deel es una plataforma de pagos, nómina y cumplimiento legal para equipos remotos, fundada en 2019 en San Francisco. Conecta a empresas que contratan talento en el exterior con freelancers y empleados que cobran desde otro país. Opera en más de 150 países, procesa pagos en más de 120 monedas y está valorada en más de 12.000 millones de dólares, con clientes como Coinbase, Shopify e Intercom. ¿Cómo funciona Deel? Cuando una empresa te contrata a través de Deel, el dinero llega a tu saldo dentro de la plataforma hasta que decides retirarlo. Tú eliges cuándo y cuánto retirar, y con qué método , lo que te da margen para esperar un tipo de cambio favorable o programar retiros automáticos. Si eres freelancer, además puedes elegir el tipo de contrato : monto fijo periódico, pago por horas trabajadas o pagos por hitos del proyecto. Cómo configurar tu método de cobro Antes de recibir tu primer pago, necesitas crear una cuenta y verificar tu identidad . El proceso es similar para freelancers y empleados con contrato. Ingresa a la web de Deel y selecciona " Sign Up ", elige la opción "I'm a contractor" o el rol que corresponda y completa tus datos personales y el tipo de trabajador que eres. Espera a que tu empleador cree y envíe el contrato, revísalo y fírmalo: allí figuran tu salario y la fecha de pago . Por último, agrega un método de retiro desde “ Finance ” > “ Withdrawal methods ”. Una vez verificada tu cuenta, puedes sumar más de un método de retiro y definir cuál usar por defecto . También puedes activar el retiro automático, elegir qué porcentaje de tu saldo se transfiere solo y dejar el resto disponible dentro de tu cuenta de Deel. Quienes necesitan liquidez antes de la fecha pactada pueden usar Advance , la función que adelanta el pago hasta 30 días antes sin pedir verificación crediticia ni cobrar intereses. Qué métodos de retiro ofrece Deel Deel ofrece más de 15 formas de retirar tu saldo, aunque la disponibilidad varía según tu país. Estas son las más comunes: Transferencia bancaria local : el dinero llega en la moneda de tu país al tipo de cambio del día. Es la opción más directa si gastas en moneda local. Transferencia internacional (SWIFT) : útil si tienes una cuenta en dólares fuera de tu país de residencia. Deel Card : tarjeta que te permite gastar directo desde tu saldo, sin esperar a que el dinero llegue a un banco. PayPal y Payoneer : retiro rápido hacia billeteras que ya usas para otros cobros. Criptomonedas : retiro en USDC o USDT a través de Coinbase, con acreditación casi inmediata. En Colombia, por ejemplo, existen más de ocho métodos disponibles, incluida la transferencia directa a Bancolombia , Davivienda o Nequi . En otros países la lista es más corta, así que conviene revisar las opciones habilitadas para tu ubicación antes de firmar el contrato. Cuánto cobra Deel por cada retiro Deel no cobra una comisión propia por la mayoría de los retiros : el costo depende del método y del banco receptor. Antes de asumir que un método es gratis, conviene revisar el detalle en tu cuenta. La Deel Card cobra 5 dólares por emitir la versión virtual y 10 dólares por la tarjeta física. Además, aplica un cargo del 1,25 % sobre cualquier compra en una moneda distinta al dólar. Si retiras en una moneda diferente a la de tu contrato, se suman tarifas de conversión que Deel no puede predecir ni controlar , porque dependen del procesador y del mercado cambiario en ese momento. Un caso particular es Ecuador : aunque el país usa dólares, no cuenta con un sistema de compensación local para esa moneda, así que cada retiro se procesa como transferencia internacional y tiene un cargo fijo de 25 dólares. Tabla de comisiones de Deel Aquí tienes una tabla comparativa de comisiones de Deel.
